title: Penn State LS Blaise Sokach-Minnich named to Mannelly Award watch list
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
The college football world is keeping a close eye on yet another Nittany Lion.

Blaise Sokach-Minnick was named to the Mannelly Award watch list, an annual award given to the nation's top long snapper.

A rising redshirt senior, Sokach-Minnick has seen action in six games thus far in his career, including two in each season from 2023-25. He is expected to be the team's starter aftering sitting behind Tyler Duzansky, who was named a finalist for the Mannelly Award last year.

If Sokach-Minnick goes the distance, he'll join Duzansky and Chris Stoll as the third finalist for the award in five years. Should he win the award, he'd follow in Stoll's footsteps as the second Penn State long snapper to earn the honor.

description:

description:

Boston drafted Stecker in the third round of the 2026 PWHL draft with the No. 27 overall pick, following her four-year stint as a Nittany Lion and a career year in 2025.

In addition to her offensive improvements, she was one of the biggest defensive anchors for the Nittany Lions not only last year, but all four years of her tenure, with more than over 80 career blocks.

Stecker showed promise and leadership across her Penn State career, and that will more than likely translate over into the pros.

description:
Ahead of the 2026 season, the hype is growing around Rocco Becht.

Becht was named to the Maxwell Award watch list on Monday, given annually to the best all-around player in college football.

He was also named to the watch list in 2025 before the award was given to Indiana national championship-winning quarterback and Heisman Trophy winner Fernando Mendoza. The last Nittany Lion to win the honor was running back Larry Johnson in 2002.

title: Off the record | The double standard of sex
author: Miss Behave I The Daily Collegian
description:
Editor’s Note: Off the record is a weekly column written by a fourth-year Collegian staffer under an alias. It aims to promote a space for honest conversations about love, sex and relationships. Those interested in sharing their experiences or submitting a topic can do so through this anonymous form.

Dear reader,

Episode 3 of Alex Cooper’s Call Her Daddy podcast has the following description: “The ultimate blow job technique that is guaranteed to be every man's kryptonite. Introducing- The Gluck Gluck 3000.”

Maybe you read the words “blow job” and were instantly thrown back to your own experience. Or maybe your body physically tensed up, not having had the topic on your roster for today: How dare I talk about, let alone open a column with, something so promiscuous?

I get it, we’ve been trained to think of anything sexual as off the table for conversation or not ladylike. But I’m not subscribing to that anymore.

Cooper, alongside other media personalities, is teaching women that talking and engaging in sex is normal, the same way it is for men. I’m sure everyone reading this can recall having to listen to a man go on and on about his latest hook-up, but can you recall doing the same?

The early days of Call Her Daddy were driven by stories about sexual encounters, mistakes and subsequent lessons her audience could learn from. Today, she conducts more formal, sit-down interviews. I can only assume the backlash she received has contributed to her new episode style, but we need the very sex talk that made Cooper famous now more than ever.

We all do it, so why is it some secret people don’t dare speak about? College, especially, is a time when people are exploring and learning, and it extends outside the classroom. I’m not saying we should be reckless in the pursuit of sex, but let’s not ignore the facts. 65% of students at Penn State are sexually active, according to a Collegian survey from February, and why shouldn’t they be? It’s a college town full of young adults who — newsflash — have sex. I’m so tired of pretending we need to tiptoe around the topic.

Do you whisper about sex? Like whispering to your friend about your other friend’s weird attitude; to your therapist about a bad thing you did last week.

I’m sure you’ve thought of it as a secret, a dirty one at that. I’m sure you’ve felt the general social pressure to pull the topic back in your throat and only let it depart from your tongue in a private space, accompanied by your closest confidants.

Well, do you whisper about how good your favorite song is? What about your favorite restaurant? I bet the answer is no.

By containing all of the same qualities as a dirty secret, sex has all the subsequent, negative associations, too. That chain reaction of something shameful:

It ends up reserved, and reserved things aren’t for public display, so reserved becomes private.

Privacy implies there’s something to hide, and hiding something implies the thing-in-hiding is bad.

I actually don’t think that society as a whole has a problem talking about sex. In fact, I think a rise in sharing personal stories on social media (and on podcasts, of course) has normalized it more, albeit only slightly. Still, when women do it, problems arise. Misogyny runs rampant. They’re subjected to every name in the book, labeled a whore, a slut, not-the-marrying-type.

I implore you to think about what a label actually does. It takes a contextualized, deeply human thing, and puts it in a box. “This is a nighttime activity.” “This is a bedroom activity.” “This is a married-people activity,” or a shameful one, or a sacred one.

But I don’t think humans find sex innately private nor shameful. We don’t come out of the womb feeling these ways about sex, yet in our society, having sex is perceived as more vulnerable than being seen crying, or being seen fail, or being seen at your worst in hundreds of other non-sexual ways.

Being overly crude is one thing when it’s uninvited, and we can definitely cross a line. Casual conversations about sex, though, aren’t hurting anyone, and they provide a space for genuine questions everyone’s probably wondering. We all had to learn from somewhere. There’s no point in being confused and left in the dark when the answers are out there, you just have to be brave enough to ask.

When it’s uncomfortable to talk to loved ones about something as intimate as sex, having spaces where people can be as unfiltered as they want proves to be a guiding light. If we don’t provide answers to women, they’ll inevitably seek them out elsewhere.

The spread of misinformation regarding sex can be extremely dangerous and easily prevented with open dialogue with women who aren’t going to be silenced just to please the social standards set before them.

Maybe the people who read this column will vehemently disagree, because it makes them uncomfortable to hear about other people's sexual experiences, or merely read the word sex. In a way, that’s exactly my point. Put on your big girl pants, grow up and stop forcing other people to act a certain way just to make you feel better. Sex isn’t a bad word.

Until next time,

Miss Behave

title: Key Penn State position battles heading into fall camp
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State will roll out a starting lineup that looks a lot different from last year, including Rocco Becht at quarterback, Carson Hansen at running back and more.

While many positions are already set for this year, there’s a number of starting spots that are still up for grabs.

Here’s a look at some position battles heading into fall camp.

Backup quarterback

Last season at Iowa State, Becht was the starting quarterback while Alex Manske held the backup spot. That duo remains, but this time at Penn State.

Unlike last year, Manske has competition for the second-string role, as the Nittany Lions brought in senior Connor Barry from Christopher Newport. With Manske recovering from an undisclosed injury and Becht rehabbing a torn labrum, Barry took a majority of starting snaps during spring ball.

The senior quarterback led the Captains to an undefeated regular season while becoming a semifinalist for the Gagliardi Trophy, which is awarded to the best Division III player, and a Second Team All-American.

However, Matt Campbell believes deeply in Manske. He said at Big Ten Media Days in Chicago that Manske has been cleared to participate in fall camp, elevating the backup quarterback battle once again.

Manske has very little collegiate experience, while Barry took a majority of first-team reps throughout the spring. If Manske can make enough of an impact over the next month, he may slot in as backup. However, Barry’s experience over the last six months gives him the slight edge heading into fall practice.

Defensive end

While young returnees Max Granville and Yvan Kemajou were both looking to start this season, Penn State’s defensive end room grew in depth during the offseason.

Campbell brought in veteran Ike Ezeogu from Iowa State and sophomore Alex McPherson from Colorado, both of whom are expected to battle for a starting spot.

Two starting jobs appear available, with all four expected to factor into the rotation. Granville will have to make a quick impact this fall after being out for almost an entire year with an undisclosed injury, while Kemajou showcased a bit of what he’s capable of toward the end of 2025.

Campbell talked about Granville’s recovery and the buzz around him returning to full health for fall camp in Chicago. Meanwhile, Anthony Donkoh praised both Granville and Kemajou for their strength and potential this season.

Left tackle

Penn State’s offensive line has just one returning starter in Donkoh at right tackle. While Trevor Buhr, Brock Riker and Cooper Cousins are expected to fill in the rest of the line, the left tackle spot is still up for competition.

Additionally, Campbell spoke with Jeff Byers on his radio show about the left tackle being a position to watch this season.

Redshirt freshman Malachi Goodman has received praise from the new staff and was the starting left tackle during the spring. At 6-foot-6, 320 pounds, the former 4-star commit has the physical traits to succeed on Ryan Clanton’s offensive line.

However, redshirt sophomore Garrett Sexton is another competitor for the role after backing up Nolan Rucci last season and filling in as the starting right tackle this spring with Donkoh sidelined. Sexton appeared in 13 games in 2025, including playing left tackle early in the year.

Also throwing his name in the hat is redshirt freshman Owen Aliciene. All three linemen were praised by Campbell throughout the spring, saying “I don't know if I could be any more impressed with what I've seen from that group.”

Defensive tackle

Unlike the defensive ends, Penn State’s defensive tackles boast numerous veterans who are competing for a starting role.

Among the older players are Keanu Williams and Siale Taupaki, who have a combined 11 years of collegiate experience. However, redshirt sophomore Armstrong Nnodim has shined during the spring and made a name for himself among the coaching staff.

Williams will likely earn a starting role after making 23 starts over the past three years with UCLA. However, the other role will likely be between Nnodim and Taupaki, as Penn State will utilize a four-down front, per Campbell in Chicago.

Nnodim has the recent momentum after starting four games last year and earning praise during the spring, but Taupaki has veteran experience and has seen the starting lineup in recent years.

description:
A former Nittany Lion is back on the coaching staff.

Former Penn State linebacker Michael Mauti has been added to the coaching staff as the director of football engagement, per the staff directory. Lions247 was the first to report the news.

Mauti played for the Nittany Lions from 2008-12 as a star linebacker, totaling a career-high 96 tackles in his final year. Across five years, Mauti recorded over 200 tackles, joining many big names in the long history of Penn State linebackers.

After his fifth season with Penn State in 2012, Mauti was selected in the seventh round of the 2013 NFL Draft by the Minnesota Vikings.

After five years in the NFL — two with the Vikings and three with the New Orleans Saints — Mauti ended his football career with 72 total tackles at the professional level.

In 2024, Mauti returned to Happy Valley as the Associate Director of Development for Intercollegiate Athletics at Penn State. Now, he returns fully to football, joining Matt Campbell's staff as another former player.

title: Penn State OL Anthony Donkoh’s off-field leadership shows strong correlation to new coaching staff
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Anthony Donkoh announced he’d return to Penn State on Dec. 30, just three days after the Nittany Lions’ Pinstripe Bowl victory over Clemson.

Now, Donkoh has emerged as a leader on the team, joining teammates Rocco Becht and Tony Rojas as Penn State’s player representatives at Big Ten Media Days, and has led by example both in the offensive line room and among the team, which has to come together in a short time for the 2026 season.

“Anthony was actually the first young man that decided to come back to Penn State when we got to campus,” Matt Campbell said at Big Ten Media Days. “Anthony's a young man whose work ethic, his character, has truly led us both on and off the football field.”

Donkoh's experience as a two-year starter and versatility allows him to better become a leader both on and off the field. While his on-field play has done a lot of talking in the past, it’s clear the redshirt junior has taken on a leadership role off the field as well, stating “it wasn’t hard” to bring the players together as one team.

Campbell’s philosophies early on have quickly aligned with how Donkoh approaches things, especially when it comes to team chemistry. The Virginia, native had a strong 2025 season, but he’s consistently remained humble in his game, something that Campbell has preached to every player through the first six months.

“If you're a humble person, people always gravitate to you easily, and that's how you walk into the room, and that's why I like him a lot as a person,” Donkoh told reporters in Chicago.

While Penn State has yet to step onto the football field in this new era, the team has been growing together as one unit. Donkoh took an approach to build bonds and connections early on in the calendar year to already have a better connection on the field even during spring practices.

“It’s better that we built the bonds fast off the field than before when we get on the field because on the field stuff can be superficial, but off the field stuff, like you're my brother, that's how it has to be, and that's how it has been. So that's been great,” Donkoh said.

With a large group of Penn State’s team coming from transfers from all over the country, Donkoh believes getting to know his teammates and growing together off the field will help the play on the field when the Nittany Lions begin their first season under Campbell in the fall.

“When you do things off the field and you guys are able to bond really well, that immediately translates to the field because you guys are building the trust and faith in those people before you even step on the field,” Donkoh said. “So, like, if something goes wrong, this is how he acts. I know how he is, and so we can be able to move forward from that, and be able to still have that same trust and faith.”

title: Former Penn Staters Saquon Barkley, Micah Parsons ranked top-10 at their positions in Madden 27
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
A pair of former Nittany Lions are top-10 players in their respective position groups in Madden 27.

EA rated Micah Parsons the No. 2 edge rusher in the game with a 98 overall and gave Saquon Barkley a 92 overall rating, making him the No. 7 running back in the game.

Now a five-year NFL veteran, Parsons is coming off his fifth-straight Pro Bowl appearance where he was third in Defensive Player of the Year voting, recording a combined 41 tackles, 12.5 sacks and 12 tackles for loss in his first season with the Green Bay Packers.

However, Parsons is currently on the sidelines after tearing his ACL in the Packers' Week 15 matchup against the Denver Broncos. Parsons is currently on the physically unable to perform list.

Parsons, who was with Penn State for the 2018 and 2019 seasons, was a consensus All-American in his sophomore season before choosing to forgo his remaining eligibility to train for the 2021 NFL Draft. He was later drafted No. 12 overall by the Dallas Cowboys.

While having a down year compared to his Super Bowl LIX winning campaign, Barkley rushed for 1,140 yards, 4.1 yards per carry and seven touchdowns in his eighth NFL regular season. He added 106 rushing yards in the Eagles playoff loss to the San Francisco 49ers.

Before becoming a three-time Pro Bowler and the 2024 Offensive Player of the Year, Barkley played college football with the Nittany Lions from 2015-17, finishing his career as the all-time leader in rushing touchdowns with 43 and total touchdowns with 53. He was drafted No. 2 overall by the New York Giants in 2018.

In Madden 26, Barkley was the cover athlete and a member of the "99 Club," one of seven players that year to have the highest rating.

title: Penn State baseball’s 2026 recruiting class ranked No. 25 nationally
author: Rafael Rivera | For the Collegian
description:
Penn State finished the 2026 recruiting cycle at No. 25 in Baseball America's post-draft signing deadline rankings, becoming the only Big Ten school to rank in the top ten.

Headlining the class is Hunter Brown, a 6-foot-5 right-handed pitcher out of North Hunterdon High School in New Jersey. According to Perfect Game Brown is the No. 1 right handed pitcher and the 9th overall player in the state, giving Penn State one of the top arms in the region.

If this is just a stopover to see how much you get paid, this is not the place.”

title: ‘You got to be in love with the process’ | How Matt Campbell’s philosophy has impacted Penn State
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Shortly after Matt Campbell became head coach at Penn State, two new signs were installed in the Lasch Building meeting room. One had four paragraphs about culture, with words like team, excellence and respect in bold, while the other listed the “Nittany Lion Code of Conduct,” encouraging saying thank you, you’re welcome and addressing people as sir and ma’am.

Over six months later, players say those principles have become some of the most noticeable changes within the program.

“Coach Campbell takes (accountability) to a whole other step,” Anthony Donkoh told reporters at Big Ten Media Days in Chicago. “This helps us build a lot of leadership, which we need to be successful on the field.”

As part of fostering leadership, Campbell created accountability groups throughout the roster. When players make mistakes on or off the field, teammates are expected to help each other learn and grow from them.

One of Campbell’s biggest messages has been that no one is above learning. Even as one of Penn State’s veteran leaders, Tony Rojas said he’s continued to lean on teammates for guidance while rehabbing from a torn ACL.

Rojas specifically said he’s had help from the leaders from Iowa State like linebacker Kooper Ebel and safety Marcus Neal Jr.

That willingness to learn extends beyond the players, with the coaching staff also molding to the team’s strengths and weaknesses and adapting its schemes to fit its personnel rather than forcing players into a rigid system.

Rojas said previous defensive coordinators often “called plays the coach wanted rather than what us players are best at.”

“I’ve had multiple different coordinators every year, so this year it’s finally where I could learn different types of defense-like schemes every year,” Rojas said. “It’s pretty easy, and coach Lynn has done a great job.”

As the Nittany Lions work toward Week 1, the players’ focus has been on team success. While several guys are projected to have breakout seasons that could improve their NFL draft stock, individual accolades have taken a back seat.

“Everybody knows that this is bigger than themselves,” Donkoh said. “At the end of the day, we need to kill our pride and be humble about things and how we move around ourselves. If you're humble, people can gravitate towards you and be able to share anything with you, and that makes sure that everybody's tight together and wants to fight for a cause.”

A big proponent of humble football is Campbell, who Donkoh described as a very modest guy. Despite making the move to a major Big Ten program Penn State, Campbell is only focused on making his team better.

As Campbell enters his first season leading the Nittany Lions, the team’s attention has stayed on the process rather than outside expectations.

“The difference I feel is this year we’re trusting the process more,” Donkoh said. “Just focus on what you can do every day to make a difference, because you got to be in love with the process. (Campbell) brings great energy and cares about your development. He’s a great coach, and I’m excited for this season.”

title: Staff predictions | Which corporation should partner with Penn State for a jersey patch?
author: The Daily Collegian Football Staff
description:
The jersey-patch era is upon college football.

Notre Dame and Ohio State announced record-breaking deals this week with SoFi and Chase Bank, respectively. The Fighting Irish are receiving somewhere from $18 to $20 million annually to sport the SoFi logo, while the Buckeyes are earning $17 million each year.

Penn State will potentially follow suit soon, as Vice President for Intercollegiate Athletics Pat Kraft told reporters in Chicago at Big Ten Media Days that the Nittany Lions are open to exploring jersey patches.

Here’s which corporations we think could ink a jersey-patch deal with Penn State in the future.

Andrew Deal: First National Bank

Penn State added a trio of stripes on July 1 with the transition to Adidas, and what better way to go all in on the “three stripe life” than with some more stripes, but this time of First National Bank’s logo.

While the Nittany Lions may not receive the sum of money that the Buckeyes or Fighting Irish are from a banking company, it could still get a large amount from a company like First National Bank.

First National Bank in particular makes sense for multiple reasons. The university announced in March its partnership with the bank, establishing it as the university’s long-term retail banking and financial services provider.

On the other hand, the logo for First National Bank features both of Penn State’s colors, blue and white. Although it has a bit of red in it — a color that’s pretty universally frowned upon at Penn State — it’s only a tiny part of the logo and can make the patch pop on the uniforms.

Other brands could make even more sense, given even closer connections to Penn State, but with First National Bank, it could garner the biggest annual payment, adding more in the pot to thrive in the new era of college football.

Andrew Mercer: Utz

When walking through the aisles of grocery stores nationwide, it’s hard not to notice the Little Utz Girl with her dark blue hair and bright red bow.

Utz would be a strong match for a jersey patch, considering Penn State’s particular emphasis on fan engagement. Spectators adore the tailgating culture of football games among other experiences where chips, pretzels and other snacks are staples of the culture. Seeing more of the Utz logo wouldn’t be out of the ordinary.

It’s a household name, particularly in the Keystone State, as the company hails from Hanover, Pennsylvania. As snacks are a common item at parties and cookouts, and the brand has a wide variety of flavors and textures, there isn’t an issue of recognition.

Utz was named the Official Potato Chip Partner of Penn State Athletics in 2018, so there’s already a concrete business link between the pair. The company also has a history of sponsoring the local professional sports teams as well, notably including the Philadelphia Phillies, Eagles and the Pittsburgh Pirates.

A simple logo of three bold letters and the iconic mascot would fit nicely on the jerseys, and it wouldn’t be so striking that it’d take away from the plain uniforms Penn State is known for.

Lexie Linderman: Hershey

Arguably the most well-known corporation in Pennsylvania is The Hershey Company, not to mention the fact that it’s one of the biggest chocolate brands in the entire world. It just makes sense to have the premier business in the state supporting the premier college athletic department.

If Penn State wants the most lucrative deal it can get, Hershey might be its best bet, considering the scope of the company. And the Nittany Lions should go after a big sum. They’re a top-10 brand in college football, so it’s only right they find a corporation that will pay them as such.

The city of Hershey is just about two hours from Penn State, so the regional ties are very much there. The Nittany Lions are also present in the community, as the football team visits Penn State Health Golisano Children's Hospital in Hershey annually.

As for how the logo would look on Penn State’s basic blues, it would look pretty clean. Hershey’s emblem is very simple, with just the company name spelled out in silver capital letters. Switch that to blue and white and it’ll blend in nicely on the home and away uniforms.

A deal with Hershey also embodies Penn State by playing into its in-state roots and the family feeling the athletic department tries to create with fans.

Noah Aberegg: Sheetz

There’s been a long-running battle between Sheetz and Wawa for the title of Pennsylvania’s favorite convenience store. What better way for Sheetz to settle that debate than by becoming a premier sponsor for one of the nation’s most recognizable college football programs?

After placing its logo on the Pittsburgh Pirates’ uniforms, Sheetz has shown it sees value in prominent sports partnerships. Adding Penn State to that portfolio would further strengthen its identity as Pennsylvania’s top gas station.

The deal may not rival the financial value of partnerships with major banks or financial technology companies, but it could resonate with Penn State’s fan base in a way few sponsors can. Sheetz has become a staple across much of Pennsylvania, making it a natural fit for the Nittany Lions.

While Sheetz’ red-and-yellow branding differs from Penn State’s traditional color palette, the logo would create a striking contrast against the Nittany Lions’ navy or white uniforms without overwhelming their classic look.

As Wawa is extending into Central Pennsylvania, a partnership with Penn State would reinforce Sheetz’s roots in the Commonwealth State while giving the Nittany Lions a sponsor that feels authentically connected to their fan base. It’s a win-win for both sides.

title: 10 classic things Penn State seniors should do before graduating
author: Justin Elliott | The Daily Collegian
description:
If you ask any Penn State graduate about their years on campus, they’ll almost certainly tell you that the four undergraduate years fly by in the blink of an eye.

Many alumni leave State College having fulfilled everything on their bucket list, while some don’t even realize they missed out on some iconic traditions until it’s too late. But don’t worry, you do have time to do it all.

Here’s 10 things Penn State seniors should check off their list before graduating.

Attending LightsUP and Movin’ On

What better way to open and close the school year than huge concerts?

LightsUP is Penn State’s student-run opening concert that’s been held on the HUB lawn at the end of August each year since 2021. Movin’ On, one of the largest student-run music festivals in the country, is the counterpart of LightsUP and an iconic send-off event held in May each year.

It’s been around for 51 years, previously featuring headliners like Sexyy Red, JID, Dayglow and, most recently, Zara Larsson.

Getting a Berkey Creamery sweet treat

An on-campus favorite, the Berkey Creamery is essential to both Penn State’s history and students’ sudden cravings for a sweet treat. The signature ice cream shop has been around for over 150 years and features flavors ranging from “Death by Chocolate” to “Peachy Paterno.”

It’s open seven days a week — much to the delight of students all over the town.

HUB lawn sledding

The borough saw absurd amounts of snowfall last winter, with the highest single-day accumulation reaching over 12 inches in January.

Though State College snow can make your fingers numb, it also provides the optimal conditions for sledding down the HUB-Robeson Center’s massive lawn. There, students can be seen taking advantage of canceled classes by sledding, throwing snowballs or making snow angels every winter.

Bar crawling

While there are only a select number of opportunities to sled on campus, there’s many more chances to participate in bar crawls throughout the school year.

Bar crawls are organized and often themed public events where participants visit a list of bars or pubs in one day, usually receiving discounts, t-shirts or costumes. Some of the most popular ones in State College are the Back to School, Santa, State Patty’s and Summer Send-Off crawls.

Hiking Mount Nittany

If you’re more into nature than bars, climbing the vast, scenic landmark known as Mount Nittany is a must. The well-preserved mountain of nearly 1,000 acres consists of over eight miles of trails for students, alumni and the simply adventurous to traverse in their free time. Whether you’re more of a casual hiker or want to test your endurance, Mount Nittany is a sight to behold.

Visiting The State Theatre

Those that are fans of the arts or avid cinephiles should visit the State Theatre at least once. The performing arts center has been in town since 1938, offering a selection of movies, musicals, live broadcasts and more at an affordable price every week throughout the year.

Keep an eye on the theatre’s weekly announcements and you’re likely to catch a classic showing.

Seeing a show at the Bryce Jordan Center

The Bryce Jordan center is a multi-purpose arena that’s not only home to the school’s Division I basketball teams, but often the venue that sees the biggest names in music and entertainment every year.

With a capacity of over 15,000 people, it’s the largest of its kind in the region, hosting names like Drake, Billie Eilish, Kane Brown and other artists as well as comedians and fine arts performers over the years. Don’t miss out on seeing arena-level stars at student-rated discounts right on campus.

Of course, going to a White Out Game

While every football game at Penn State is bound to be one of the more electric experiences one can get at the school, the annual “White Out” game is undoubtedly the most highly anticipated one each year.

Whether you’re at the game — which often attracts crowds of over 100,000 people — at the tailgates, or downtown, the energy in State College on the day of White Out is one every student should feel before graduating.

Arts Fest-ing

Unless you’re taking a summer class, you may not see much reason to visit State College in the summer. If you’re into the arts, however, you might want to consider returning in July.

Every summer, the Central Pennsylvania Festival of the Arts comes to town, and a resurgence of over 100,000 visitors with it. From paintings to performances, hundreds of artists bring original work, tucked into tents or lining the streets.

THON

The Penn State Dance Marathon, better known as THON, is perhaps the most uniting event of the year in State College for students.

Over 16,000 student volunteers participate in nonstop dancing and activities for 46 hours straight, fundraising millions of dollars each year to fight childhood cancer. The Bryce Jordan Center comes alive with student organizations, long lines, food and live music as the community unites “For The Kids.”

Whether you’re participating or supporting, THON is a one-of-a-kind event for students to attend before graduating.

title: What to know as Mount Nittany workers enter fourth day of strike
author: Grace Levy | The Daily Collegian
description:
On Monday, union employees represented by SEIU Healthcare Pennsylvania began a planned five-day strike at Mount Nittany Medical Center.

Here’s what to know as the strike enters its fourth day.

How many people are on strike?

According to SEIU Healthcare Pennsylvania, 950 workers — nurses and staff members represented by the union — are on strike.

But members of other local unions have also joined the picket line in support of the Mount Nittany workers, including members of the teachers, steelworkers, bricklayers, electrical and teamsters unions.

Why are they striking?

In a Facebook post, SEIU Healthcare Pennsylvania said its top priorities are “fair wages that recruit and retain experienced workers for community care as well as improvements in workplace and patient safety.”

“They have been struggling to support their families with the spiraling costs of living in Centre County, and Mount Nittany executives have not even offered raises that cover inflation,” the post read.

Fawn Guignet, an ER nurse and member of the union’s bargaining committee, has worked at Mount Nittany for over 10 years. She said she worked as a monitor clerk before finishing nursing school last year, which helped her understand the importance of having support staff.

“They don't feel that we deserve even a living wage, let alone enough to meet inflation. That's the big thing,” Guignet said. “They need to still be able to afford to work here and to be part of our patient care team.”

SEIU Healthcare Pennsylvania’s post also said Mount Nittany is the fourth most profitable hospital in the state with over 30% profit margins, and “has more than enough resources to reach an agreement that invests in all employees responsible for providing renowned care.”

“The majority of people who work here don't even live in Centre County just because the cost of living in this part of the state is so expensive. The cost of living is comparable to that of Pittsburgh,” Jenna Cowan, a medical laboratory scientist and union chapter vice president, said. “They haven’t given us a wage increase to match the cost of inflation.”

The average cost of purchasing a home in Centre County has nearly doubled since 2017, a disparity more pronounced in regions closest to State College, according to the Centre Daily Times.

Unionized employees and Mount Nittany Medical Center executives have been in the negotiating process for a new labor contract since April 29. The last contract expired June 30, and union members voted in favor of a strike on July 2.

During a July 21 negotiation meeting, Mount Nittany offered a one-year contract extension; three percent across-the-board wage increase for all union members; $1,000 ratification bonus for every bargaining unit employee; wage scale upgrades for 18 job classifications; and continued investments in workplace safety in their most recent proposal, according to the Mount Nittany Health website.

The union rejected this offer, saying it is not a fair increase, WPSU reported.

How long will the strike last?

The strike will continue until Saturday at 7 a.m. Contract negotiations are expected to resume after the strike.

“We're just ready to get back inside. We want to get a contract,” Josh Rosefsky, an utility specialist in maintenance and member of the union’s negotiating committee, said. “We're ready to negotiate as soon as they get the authority to actually move on their wages, because that's the big thing, where they keep getting told that they don't have the authority to move on anything.”

Rosefsky said the negotiations are for all employees, rather than just one individual department.

“The hospital tried to split us up. They wanted better raises for nurses and not everybody else. Our entire membership, they didn’t want that,” Rosefsky said. “This hospital does not run just on nurses. It is environmental services. It is respiratory. It is the kitchen. It’s lab, imaging, it's ED nurses, it’s regular nurses.”

Are patients affected by the strike?

People with scheduled appointments, procedures and treatments should plan to attend unless contacted directly by a member of their care team, according to Mount Nittany’s website.

The emergency department will remain open.

Select outpatient labs and imaging locations will have temporary changes to their hours during the duration of the strike.

Select locations will be closed throughout the strike. This includes:

title: ‘I just can't wait’ | Penn State QB Rocco Becht, now fully healthy, is eager to get back on the field
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
When Rocco Becht arrived on campus, he was limited in his throwing reps due to lingering injuries to both of his shoulders. While he used the time to curate personal connections with his new teammates, he lost out on live reps this spring.

But now, Becht is itching to go. The winningest quarterback returning to college football revealed at Big Ten Media Days in Chicago that he’s fully healthy and expressed his gratitude for everyone who helped him through the process as well.

“Recovery's going great,” Becht told reporters in Chicago. “The training staff and the waiver staff have done a great job with me. Not just me, but everyone on our team that's been injured. But yeah, I'm super anxious for college football to be back, really fall camp because I wasn't able to do a lot in spring. But I just can't wait to go back out there.”

Campbell took the time to speak about Becht’s character while he was up on the podium at Big Ten Media Days, telling the audience that he’s earned everything he’s accomplished, with his grit, character and toughness leading the way.

Becht has already shown those traits in his few months as a Nittany Lion. While he couldn’t make an impact on the field this spring, he chose to establish himself as a leader in the locker room, helping forge bonds between former Cyclones and the Penn State returnees.

“I think to win games to succeed in college football, you got to have those bonds. You can't just have relationships with me as you know a quarterback to a quarterback, quarterback to a receiver,” Becht said. “I got to have relationships with everyone. The D line, the corners, the linebackers, and that's something that I've been able to work on.”

Throughout the spring and summer, Campbell brought back a series of Penn State lettermen to speak with the team. Becht got to learn from past star Nittany Lion gunslingers such as Todd Blackledge, Trace McSorley, Christian Hackenberg and Kerry Collins about the unique position he’s entered — the pressures, expectations and realities of being a Penn State quarterback.

“Being able to speak to those guys about how to be a Penn State quarterback is something that I've been able to instill in myself over the past summer,” Becht said. “Hopefully being able to go out there and play like a Penn State quarterback this season.”

Even his nickname, “Mr. President,” allegedly coined by wide receiver Chase Sowell, is something that he doesn’t let go to his head, although Becht thinks it’s “pretty funny.”

With Becht, Sowell, Brett Eskildsen, Koby Howard and the rest of the offense now fully healthy, Penn State has no limitations on that side of the ball, and Becht is optimistic about where the Nittany Lions can go from here.

“​​The chemistry is there,” Becht said. “Fall camp is kind of just that exclamation point of putting everything together before the season.”

title: ‘It was a humongous blessing’ | Penn State players reflect on team bonding at weekend retreat
author: Lexie Linderman | Football Editor
description:
When Matt Campbell first shared what Penn State would be doing last weekend, Tony Rojas was a bit skeptical.

But he and the rest of the Nittany Lions’ leaders knew spending the weekend in Pine Valley would only help them become closer as a team — something that remains so crucial as the melting pot that is Penn State has just over a month until everything needs to be put together on the field.

“It was a bonding experience. Got to know each other more. We had late night talks and s’mores,” Rojas told reporters at Big Ten Media Days in Chicago. “It was funny, interesting, and it was just a great time. I learned a lot about my teammates, and we got to just open up, which I think is important for the season, and we just got to know each other deeply, way better.”

For the retreat, the team was split up into groups of 12, and each group stayed in their own cabin with bunk bends. Rojas said the experience reminded him of the movie ‘Annie.’

The first night, the Nittany Lions gathered into their leadership teams around the campfire and spoke with the younger players about what they have and haven’t liked from the veterans so far, which Rojas said was “great.”

Oh, and Marcus Neal Jr., Donnie Harbour, Armstrong Nnodim and Yvan Kemajou had a rap battle. Anthony Donkoh said Nnodim and Kemajou each won once.

It was the next day, however, that Penn State made a difference in the community, which has been a big emphasis under Campbell. Rojas said about 80 underprivileged children joined them for the day, playing some basketball, fishing and swimming in the pool.

“Sometimes we got to put the helmet down and be people outside of the helmet,” Rojas said. “So I think being able to give back to the community with just a chance to give back to the less fortunate, because obviously with NIL, we should be able to give back, and I think that's the biggest thing.”

All the coaches also enjoyed the retreat. Rojas said a few of them, including D’Anton Lynn, spoke about “why they’re doing this and how they could help us.”

But Donkoh said Campbell enjoyed it the most of all, with his competitive nature even coming out in an attempt to make a bigger wave off the slide than one of the teams of 12.

“He was loving it because he was happy that we all had a good time, and like he meant for it to be a good time for us. So he achieved what he wanted to achieve,” Donkoh said. “It was pretty cool and fun to see him interact with us and be with us and that stuff.”

The real takeaway from the retreat was the deeper bonds between the players that formed, and Donkoh feels they now have connections that will translate easily to the field this fall.

“It was one of those things that was just like ‘yeah we needed this,’ because like we need as much as we can to be around each other,” Donkoh said. “Especially right before the season, we need something like this so we went to go do it. It was a humongous blessing. Everybody had a fun time. It was amazing

title: Penn State notebook | Matt Campbell talks leadership, tradition at first Big Ten Media Days
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Matt Campbell will coach his first game at Penn State in just over a month as the season quickly approaches, and the first deal of business to start the fall season took place in Chicago.

Campbell took the stand at Big Ten Media Days to discuss early leadership in the program, a new defensive system and the tradition of Penn State both on and off the field.

Here’s what Campbell had to say at his first Big Ten Media Days.

Leadership emerged quickly

Despite large roster turnover, Penn State has a high number of seniors who’ve helped turn a group of players into a team in a short amount of time. Among those are Anthony Donkoh, Rocco Becht and Tony Rojas.

“These young men are part of 24 seniors who have led the way from Day 1 since we came back in January, of building the standard and expectation of moving our football program forward,” Campbell said.

Donkoh rotated around the offensive line during his two seasons as a starter at Penn State and was the key first player to make his decision to return following the hiring of Campbell. Since then he’s become an instrumental leader “whose work ethic, his character, has truly led us both on and off the football field.”

Penn State’s projected starting quarterback, Becht enters with the most experience of any returning gunslinger. Although he’s on a new team, Becht’s leadership hasn’t wavered in the first six months in Happy Valley.

“Rocco is one of the young men whose grit, whose character, whose toughness has led the way during his college football career, and he's earned the right to be great every step of the way, and in a short amount of time, has been an unbelievable competitor and connector in our locker room,” Campbell said.

Rojas, like Becht, is returning from a major injury, and is a full go for the start of camp. Despite not being on the field at all during spring practices and workouts, Rojas is another player whose hard work stood out to Campbell, especially off the field.

“It's a small sample of a locker room of gentlemen just like them, a locker room of young men that stayed at Penn State, and a locker room of young men that came to Penn State for a devoted cause, and we keep talking about this devoted cause of building one team, a team that has great standards and expectations for themselves, a team that understands the value that nothing is guaranteed,” Campbell said.

D’Anton Lynn, defensive scheme

D’Anton Lynn is back at Penn State, this time as a coach and will be leading the defense. Before Penn State, he made stops at USC and UCLA, turning both defenses around and understanding the type of defense needed to succeed in the Big Ten.

Lynn’s added history of playing with the Nittany Lions, from 2008-11, made the hire even more critical for Campbell’s staff in his first year.

“He's a former player, and he understands what it means to play at Penn State,” Campbell said. “He understands what it means to lead at Penn State, and he and his family have a deep passion for the community and the success of the Penn State football program.”

In his short time already at Penn State, Lynn’s implemented a different defense than what Campbell’s units were playing in at Iowa State and has already “had a profound impact on the young men in our program.”

Lynn’s defense will feature a four-down front, whereas the defense at Iowa State under Campbell was a 3-3-5, which still found a lot of success. The decision to switch to a more four-down front wasn’t that difficult given the personnel and what the staff wants the defense to be.

“I still think the ability to have multiplicity in what we do defensively is certainly critical, but maybe coming from it with more of a four down front,” Campbell said. “But I still think those multiple variables are huge.”

Penn State tradition

The Nittany Lions are littered with tradition and historic players dating back to the 19th century, and the emphasis to lean into that has been strong from Campbell and his staff.

Penn State’s Adidas rollout showed how historic the program’s brand is, as the uniforms saw zero changes to its notorious basic blues.

“The history, the legacy we represent, it's deep,” Campbell said. “It's deep with great coaches. It's deep with great players, and certainly deep with tremendous and great teams, some of the best that have ever played in college football. It's an honor to build on those great successes and traditions of our past.”

One of the ways Campbell has already dipped into the tradition is by keeping Terry Smith on staff. Smith played at Penn State, who had a long history of success coaching at the high school level in Pennsylvania before joining the Nittany Lions.

Smith led Penn State as the interim head coach following the firing of James Franklin, helping the team win the Pinstripe Bowl to cap off a 7-6 season.

“Terry did a great job settling the ship and giving us a great foundation to move forward from,” Campbell said. “So my gratitude and honor to be able to work forward with Terry and lead forward with Terry means a great deal to myself, and certainly means a great deal to our young men in our football program.”

title: 4 storylines to watch as Penn State begins fall camp
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s fall camp is almost here, and Matt Campbell’s squad has just over a month left to prepare for the 2026 season.

The Nittany Lions are entering a demanding stretch of time. Position battles will be settled, injured players are slated to return and this is the moment for the coaching staff to put hammer to nail so the team is ready when Marshall comes knocking on Week 1.

Here are a few storylines to follow heading into fall camp.

The running back saga

Penn State’s previous offensive core under James Franklin was defined by its backfield tandem of Nick Singleton and Kaytron Allen.

In Campbell’s case, his running back room under Savon Huggins has the potential to bring back a similar rotation. He brought Carson Hansen with him from Iowa State, who’d been Campbell’s go-to for the past three seasons, and James Peoples, who transferred in from Ohio State.

Peoples filled the Buckeyes’ third-string role, and Quinton Martin Jr. made a name for himself by 103 rushing yards in the Pinstripe Bowl victory over Clemson last year when Singleton and Allen opted out.

Hansen and Peoples will likely get the bulk of the touches depending on the situation with Martin filling the gaps. However, one may use fall camp to establish themself as the No. 1.

“That's going to be great competition all the way through fall camp,” Campbell said in April. “But I think the one thing is all three have shown really great things.”

Is the offense fully meshed?

Iowa State transfers Chase Sowell and Brett Eskildsen were limited throughout spring ball, leading to fall camp being the last stretch of opportunity for the offense to fully adjust to the new surroundings before the season kicks off.

Koby Howard, returning for his second season as a Nittany Lion, is set to make a greater impact. He showed promise after Franklin’s firing when Terry Smith gave him more playing time and later impressed Campbell with a strong showing in the spring.

While the offensive skill players are mostly former Cyclones, including projected starting tight end Benjamin Brahmer, there’s returner Andrew Rappleyea who’ll continue to adjust to his new teammates after returning from a lower body injury that kept him off the field this spring.

It’ll be interesting to see how Howard and Rappleyea adapt to playing alongside the former Iowa State personnel, and how they mesh with Mouser’s playcalling.

D’Anton Lynn’s defensive scheme

All spring long, D’Anton Lynn has preached a “slow installation” of his defensive systems to ensure that all of his players have a fundamental understanding of the scheme and nobody is confused.

“We’ve tried to install slowly with the guys, equal amount of reps and different concepts, just to see,” Lynn said in April. “But the one thing you see, the guys fly around, the guys communicate, and the guys know a lot of ball.”

However, the question is about the progress here and now: How well does the defense mesh with Lynn’s system?

Last year, there were struggles to comprehend and execute Jim Knowles’ notably intricate playbook, which led to defensive lapses. That’s the last thing Lynn wants to happen in his first season as Penn State’s defensive coordinator, and he has one last period to get everyone up to speed during fall camp.

Tony Rojas and Jeremiah Cooper

Two of Penn State’s defensive standouts are coming back from torn ACLs. Both Rojas and Cooper were injured early last season when they were each primed to make a splash.

Now, the pair are expected to return and be cornerstones of the Nittany Lions’ defense. But the question is this: will they show the rust in Week 1 or will all the kinks be worked out in training camp?

Rojas and Cooper didn’t see live reps throughout the spring, but are likely still slated to return for the season opener. So, fall camp will have to be expedited to get the pair working in practical situations.

“You're going to have injuries, and you're going to have guys coming back from season-ending injuries, and some of those are our major, some of those are clean up,” Campbell said ahead of spring ball. “I think from my end (going) slow and right with anybody that's coming off of an injury is still priority No. 1.”

title: Penn State track and field implications from Ryan Foster departure
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Earlier this month, shockwaves rippled through the collegiate track and field world as former Penn State associate head coach and middle-distance coach Ryan Foster left for the same role at Auburn.

Foster, a 2011 Penn State graduate and four-time Big Ten champion, spent the last five years building one of the nation’s premier middle-distance programs alongside his wife, Kara Foster.

Since Foster’s departure, multiple recruits have decommitted from Penn State, transfer speculation has emerged and questions remain about the future of the Nittany Lions’ middle-distance program.

Here’s a look at some implications as Penn State’s “800-meter U” title is now in jeopardy.

Recruiting fallout

The Nittany Lions were set to welcome one of the biggest recruiting classes in many years, highlighted by three standout 800m recruits.

Among the athletes previously committed to Penn State were Joshua Sharp, the 2026 Under Armour 800m national champion, and Raynier Galvez, the NJCAA 800m champion and NJCAA Athlete of the Year.

Since Foster’s departure for Auburn, both athletes have decommitted from Penn State. Less than a week after the news broke, Sharp committed to Auburn. His commitment post included a photo of him and Galvez in Auburn uniforms from their official visit.

Galvez has yet to commit to the Tigers, as he announced he’s also looking at Kansas State, which recently hired his former coach at Indian Hills Community College.

Losing both recruits further depletes Penn State’s 800m depth. The Nittany Lions already lost Niko Schultz, Yukichi Ishii and Allon Clay to graduation, all of whom rank among the top-10 in school history for indoor and outdoor 800m.

Galvez set a personal-best mark of 1:44.14 in April, which would be a school record for Penn State. Meanwhile, Sharp’s mark of 1:47.22 would rank just outside the top 10.

Penn State still has a commitment from star Australian runner Daniel Williams, who holds a personal best 1:44.37 and recently won the Australian U20 championships. Williams was recruited by Foster, leaving uncertainty about whether the coaching change could affect his commitment.

Potential transfers

Despite losing several recruits to Auburn and other athletes to graduation, Penn State still has a strong 800m unit on both the men’s and women’s side.

However, many of those athletes came to Happy Valley because of Foster and found success under his coaching. Some could consider transferring to Auburn to work with him.

After redshirting during the 2026 outdoor season and 2025 indoor season — the latter due to injury — Handal Roban is set to return to Happy Valley for a full year. He set both the indoor and outdoor school records under Foster, and is expected to be a top competitor for this year’s national title.

On the women’s side, Hayley Kitching has one outdoor season of eligibility remaining. She’s coming off a second-place finish at the NCAA Championships, and with her also being from Australia, could consider following Foster to Auburn for one final season.

Both Boh Ritchie and Tayissa Buchanan are young runners with regional ties to Foster, with Ritchie coming from New Zealand and Buchanan from Australia. The duo both hold top-10 marks in the indoor and outdoor record book and could look to Foster for additional coaching.

While rising senior Andrew Regnier was part of Penn State’s “800m U” success last year, he only competed one season for Foster, making his situation somewhat different from several of Foster’s longer-tenured athletes. Still, he was a major part in Regnier’s decision to transfer to Penn State.

Future outlook

Foster has spent eight seasons on Penn State’s coaching staff after competing for four as a Nittany Lion. He’s developed Penn State into one of the nation’s top middle-distance programs, which has continued to improve every year.

Head coach John Gondak is entering his 31st season as a collegiate coach and is in his early 50s. Although Gondak has given no indication that retirement is imminent, succession planning is a reality for every long-tenured program.

Foster appeared to fit the profile of a potential future Penn State head coach after transforming Penn State’s recruiting efforts and helping establish the program as a national contender.

He likely would’ve been a strong internal candidate whenever Gondak eventually stepped aside. Whether Penn State can maintain the momentum Foster helped build will become clearer over the coming months as recruiting decisions, roster movement and the upcoming season unfold.

title: Mike Rhoades names 3 Penn State men’s basketball players as summer standouts
author: Will Horstman | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State is three quarters of the way through summer practices after an offseason full of roster turnover. So far, the Nittany Lions have officially added nine new players.

With that change brings new faces into Penn State’s practice gym, and Mike Rhoades mentioned three players who’ve stuck out to him during a recent press conference via a Zoom call.

Here’s who Rhoades named, in order.

Roberts Blums

Not only did Rhoades mention Davidson transfer Roberts Blums first, he also doubled down on it at the end of his answer by saying Blums “would be at the top of that list.”

“He's just my type of guy,” Rhoades said. “He's my type of guard. He's just super competitive, works so hard, so into it. I knew he was a good player coming from a good program like Davidson.”

Blums helped fill two of the Nittany Lions’ main needs this offseason: experience and 3-point shooting. He played in 63 games through his first two collegiate years at Davidson, where he shot 40.7% from 3-point range last season.

The 6-foot-4, 190-pounder is projected starter at shooting guard for Penn State this upcoming season. He’s received other offseason recognition, as after Week 1 of summer practices, he was the Wild Lion of the Week, a weekly team award given out to the player who exhibits the most effort.

“He can make plays,” Rhoades said. “He knows how to. He plays super hard, he's about the right stuff, he's a great voice in practice. I've been really pleased with him.”

Thomas Allard

Guard Thomas Allard is making a significant jump in competition from the Division II level to the Big Ten, but he still got a mention from Rhoades.

“He's a guy that's probably played 120 college games under his belt,” Rhoades said. “He can dribble, shoot and pass at a high level. He gets it. He knows how to play the right way. I've been really, really fired up with him.”

Allard is heading into his final year of eligibility after spending last season at the University of Alabama-Huntsville, and three years before that at Lincoln Memorial University. Having that amount of collegiate experience is seemingly helping him with the Nittany Lions, and he has size for a guard at 6-foot-7 and 210 pounds.

The Suwanee, Georgia, native averaged 13.7 points, 4.9 rebounds and 3.5 assists per game while making 32 starts en route to Alabama-Huntsville’s appearance in the NCAA Division II Sweet 16 last season. Allard, who was the Wild Lion of the Week during Week 4 of summer practices, could provide solid depth behind Blums at shooting guard for Penn State.

Dasonte Bowen

Even after adding Central Connecticut State transfer Jay Rodgers, Penn State still needed another point guard this offseason. Rhoades then found one in St. Bonaventure transfer Dasonte Bowen, who was a late addition by signing during Week 2 of summer practices.

“Dasonte showed up, had to wait till all his medical testing, and then by the second day he was here, (he started) making an impact, making an impact on the team,” Rhoades said.

Bowen, who averaged 10.9 points and 4.8 assists per game last season, is another experienced guard for Rhoades. He’s going into his fifth season, and he started his career in the Big Ten at Iowa.

Rodgers was presumed to be the starting point guard when he transferred to the Nittany Lions in April. However, Bowen, who was the Wild Lion of the Week after Week 5 and 6 of summer practices, seems to be making a push for the job.

title: Penn State men's hockey's Smith, Busch selected for 2026 World Junior Summer Showcase

Sophomore defenseman Jackson Smith and incoming freshman forward Shea Busch have been invited to the 2026 World Junior Summer Showcase by Hockey Canada, the first step in the selection process for Canada's 2027 IIHF World Junior Championship team.

Smith, a Calgary, Alberta, native, and Busch, a North Vancouver, British Columbia, native, will participate in practices and exhibition games against the United States, Sweden and Finland. They’ll then return to Penn State for the upcoming season and hope to be invited to the final selection camp in December.

Smith is familiar with representing Canada in international tournaments, as he played a key role in winning gold at the 2025 IIHF U18 World Championship. Busch, however, has yet to be a part of Canada’s World Junior pipeline.

After being selected No. 14 overall in the 2025 NHL Draft, becoming Penn State's first ever first-round draft pick, Smith had a phenomenal freshman campaign.

He solidified himself as one of the nation's best offensive defenseman, notching 26 points, 11 goals, and 15 assists. Following the season, he was honored with accolades such as All-Big Ten Second Team and Big Ten All-Freshman Team.

Busch, who was selected in the fourth round of that same draft to the Florida Panthers, had just as impressive a season for the Everett Silvertips of the Western Hockey League.

Although he suffered an upper-body injury that kept him out for several months of the season, he still played a major role in the Silvertips’ first WHL championship in franchise history. He scored 7 goals and 6 assists in 16 postseason games.

Now, Smith and Busch will showcase their talents in front of Hockey Canada’s national team staff, NHL scouts, and representatives from their respective NHL teams as they compete for a spot on one of the most prestigious international hockey teams in the world.

title: Exploring Matt Campbell’s collegiate coaching tree
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Across Matt Campbell’s 15-year head coaching career, he transformed programs from bottom dwellers to conference championship contenders.

Along the way, he’s also developed numerous assistant coaches who’ve found success of their own. Some have stuck with Campbell for many years, while others have gone off to lead programs of their own or take their talents to the NFL.

Here’s a look at several of Campbell’s former coaches, the successes they’ve had and where they are now.

Alex Golesh

Campbell and Alex Golesh first crossed paths in 2009 at Toledo, where they each served as position coaches for the Rockets. Over the next few years, Campbell earned numerous promotions — including to head coach in 2012 — while Golesh departed for Illinois that same year.

When Campbell was named head coach for Iowa State in 2016, he brought Golesh to serve as tight ends coach, a position he had held since 2010 with Illinois.

After four years with the Cyclones, Golesh earned his first coordinator position at UCF, serving as co-offensive coordinator and tight ends coach for one season. In 2021, he became the offensive coordinator at Tennessee, setting eight single-season records on offense in Year 1 before finishing as the highest scoring offense in the nation the following season.

Golesh’ first head coaching role came at South Florida, where he brought the Bulls from four wins in three years to back-to-back seven-win seasons and a pair of bowl victories. His third season saw a near 10-year best of nine wins and No. 18 spot in the AP Poll during 2025.

In December, Golesh was hired as the next head coach at Auburn, as Campbell praised his former assistant, saying, “Alex is a terrific leader. He cares about his players and elevates those around him.”

Nate Scheelhaase

Following a playing and early coaching career at Illinois, Nate Scheelhaase joined Campbell’s squad at Iowa State as the running backs coach. In his first season, he mentored David Montgomery to an All-American season, later going on to be a star running back in the NFL.

Scheelhaase bounced between numerous roles with the Cyclones en route to being offensive coordinator in 2023, a position he held for two years. During that time, he received numerous awards and nominations, including a place on 247Sports’ “30Under30” and a spot as a finalist for FootballScoop.com’s Wide Receiver Coach of the Year.

With Scheelhaase aiding the offense, Iowa State recorded three of the best offensive campaigns in school history, including the school record for most offensive yardage in 2019.

In 2024, Scheelhaase took his talents to the NFL, where he served as an offensive assistant and pass game specialist for the Los Angeles Rams, earning multiple top-10 offensive marks.

The following year, Scheelhaase was promoted to pass game coordinator, mentoring Stafford to an MVP award, resulting in multiple interviews for open head coaching spots. He’ll take the sidelines for his biggest role yet this year, as was named offensive coordinator in February.

Jason Candle

Jason Candle and Matt Campbell took the field together at Mount Union for two years to conclude their collegiate careers. In 2009, the duo was reunited at Toledo, as Candle served in various positions coaching receivers and tight ends.

After Campbell became head coach in 2012, Candle was promoted to offensive coordinator. The offense saw major improvements under Candle, aiding in the team’s 36-15 record over four years. In 2014, he was named associate head coach.

Following Campbell’s departure to Iowa State, Candle was promoted to head coach, where he coached his squad to a pair of 11-win seasons and three bowl victories over his 10-year stint. He became the winningest head coach in school history, claiming three conference titles in the process.

In December, Candle was announced as the next head coach at UConn, ending his long and historic career with the Rockets.

Tom Manning

Also with ties to Mount Union, Tom Manning’s Division I coaching career began with Campbell at Toledo, where he started as a graduate assistant.

The following season, Manning was promoted to director of football operations with the Rockets before returning to Mount Union as the offensive line coach. In 2012, he rejoined Campbell at Toledo and served as the offensive line coach for three seasons, before serving as offensive coordinator and offensive line coach at Iowa State for two seasons.

In 2018, Manning made the leap to the NFL, where he became the tight ends coach for the Indianapolis Colts. After just one season, he once again rejoined Campbell in Ames.

After four more years at Iowa State, Manning returned to Indianapolis, where he’s been since 2023. Most recently, he coached former Penn State tight end Tyler Warren to the fifth-most receiving yards among tight ends.

title: Lights, posters | 5 items to make your dorm your own
author: Sarah Price | For The Collegian
description:
Penn State students are a month away from returning to campus for the fall semester. As the time dwindles down, so should your dorm shopping list. While the necessities may be easy to buy, decorations can be overwhelming.

Here are five items to help make your dorm yours.

Lights, lights and more lights

The dorm lights are bright and, frankly, not very well lit.

A fun yet practical way to personalize your dorm is through a variety of lamps. A desk lamp is a necessity for late-night studying. Your roommate will appreciate the dim lighting while you’re cramming for your math exam. A bedside lamp can help you during your bedtime scrolling or reading for class the next morning.

Be sure to purchase as many small lamps, string lights and desk lights as possible to create a warm and cozy atmosphere.

String lights come in a variety of lengths, colors and sometimes clips to hang photos. It’ll make your dorm room the ultimate hangout spot with dim lighting that makes it pleasing to look at.

While some students may prefer the big light, lamps and string lights can really make your Penn State dorm feel like home.

State College decor

It is almost mandatory for every student to have at least one piece of State College decor, and it doesn’t require a purchase.

You can start by collecting items from football games, like the pom-pom’s from the student section, or the swag you collect during Welcome Week.

That said, if you’d like to purchase State College decor, you can always find something downtown. Take a walk down East College Avenue, and you’ll be sure to take home a piece of State College decor.

Decorative pillows and blankets

A simple way to make your dorm feel more comfortable while also looking stylish is by adding decorative throw pillows and blankets to your bed.

You can shop for affordable throw pillows at TJMaxx, which offers a wide variety of shapes, sizes and designs to fit any dorm theme. While there, you can also shop for a throw blanket that will give your bedding an extra pop of color.

Although it does require a bit of upkeep (a.k.a. making your bed every morning). If you know you won’t keep up with it, then maybe stick to your typical bedding.

Movie posters

To decorate the walls, you can never go wrong with movie posters. It’s a simple and easy way to showcase your favorite movies.

For those who like to plan ahead, you can easily find a variety of movie posters online and print them at your local CVS or Walmart.

If you get to campus and still need to fill some wall space, check out the poster sale at the HUB during the first week of classes. They offer a variety of genres and sizes to fit any type of space.

LEGO sets

If you have pre-built LEGO sets at home, they make great decorations for dorms, and it doesn’t require an extra purchase. Be sure to pack your LEGO sets with extra care and protection to ensure they don’t break during your travel to campus.

However, if you’re in the market for either your first set or a new one, you can find LEGO at Growing Tree Toys located at the corner of West Beaver Avenue and South Allen Street.

LEGO sets serve multiple purposes as well — they can be a fun activity with friends or a partner and also serve as a unique decoration. The sets in your dorm can show off your personality and interests, so choose wisely.

Framed photos

For the incoming first years, adding a piece of home to your dorm makes the big change feel more comforting. Be sure to include your family in your room, as they’ve likely been there from the beginning.

For those returning to campus this fall, include Penn State memories, and always leave room for more to come.

title: Penn State men’s basketball notebook | Coach Mike Rhoades, players Brant Byers, Ivan Jurić discuss offseason
author: Myles Hannak | The Daily Collegian
description:
For the first time this offseason, Penn State was available to the media on Tuesday, with coach Mike Rhoades and players Ivan Jurić and Brant Byers in front of a packed Zoom meeting.

The blue and white has had a revolving door of personnel changes through the transfer portal, resulting in a completely overhauled roster. The coach and players addressed the new-look Nittany Lions, their development and the season ahead on Tuesday.

Here’s all that and more from a lengthy address.

New identity, team building

It’s no secret that the blue and white looks different this season. What was one of the youngest squads in the conference a season ago has gotten a veteran injection through the portal, resulting in a new feel in a squad where identity hasn’t been widely established yet.

“We’re going to play differently than I’ve done in the past, probably more like I played at Randolph-Macon and at Rice because we just want to have the depth of talent that other teams have,” Rhoades said. “I think at this level in the Big Ten, when everybody is bigger and older, and there’s unbelievable depth, you gotta be able to finish plays with whoever you have out there. That’s probably one of my biggest emphases going into this year, making sure we defend and execute and really finish plays to give ourselves a chance to be successful.”

Despite a clear interior direction of where the Nittany Lions are headed, it all starts with the process. Rhoades peeled back the curtain on what they’ve been doing this summer to get to that point, noting a heavy focus on the weight room and a tailored coaching style to each player’s needs.

Rhoades also revealed some of the team’s extracurriculars from this summer that are meant to change the approach and grow chemistry-building efforts. He said he had the team at his house for a cooking class, and they have an upcoming paintball tournament.

“I think building that in our culture is more important than just the leadership part. The leadership part will start coming when we get back to school, and certain guys that have the ball in their hands and are on the court and have the biggest voices will take over, and we’re going to build that together,” Rhoades said.

Player personnel

While Rhoades heavily discussed the unit as a whole, it’s no secret that there are a few players that stand out in the bunch as integral to their success next season. The crown jewel of it all was the Miami (OH) addition, Brant Byers, who had made it to the NCAA Tournament after averaging 14.2 points per game last season.

“Two things that I think stand out the most is that (Byers) was really excited to come back home and be back in Pennsylvania,” Rhoades said. “He and his family and his agent did their homework on Penn State and how I do things and how we play and all that stuff and I think he saw the fit, which I think is huge, understanding the fit.”

Byers, a Chambersburg, Pennsylvania, native, noted the awe of being on campus and even named Tony Carr and Andrew Funk as his favorite Penn State players all-time.

Despite him representing an unprecedented marquee addition for the program, his talent on the surface was clear. When quizzed on players who had surprised him early, Rhoades gave insight on whose talent may not have been initially present.

“I knew (Roberts Blums) was a good player coming from a good program like Davidson. He was gonna have a lot of things that we were gonna like, but he’s taken it to a whole other level,” Rhoades said.

Rhoades gave props to two fellow transfer guard additions for their displays early, but fans will have to wait to see how the depth chart fills out alongside Central Connecticut transfer point guard Jay Rodgers, freshman Andy Gemao and returnee redshirt freshman Reggie Grodin.

“Thomas Allard, a Division II player … he’s a guy that’s probably played 120 college games under his belt. He can dribble, shoot and pass at a high level. He gets it. He knows how to play the right way. I’ve been really fired up with him,” Rhoades said. “Dasonte (Bowen) showed up, had to wait until all his medical testing, and then by the second day he was here making an impact.”

With Byers holding firm on the wing, the questions turned to how 7-footers Ivan Jurić and Memphis transfer Tim Oboh would slot in alongside each other.

“In practices, sometimes when we play against each other, we both play fives, and then if we play together, we can switch forwards and fives,” Jurić said. “Depends on what we’re doing, but I think we complement each other really well because of how different our skill sets are.”

Program, sport landscape

With college sports at a whirlwind by most metrics, almost no university, conference, player or coach seems immune from the noise.

The 5-for-5 rule, which allows athletes five years of eligibility post-graduation, is impacting those who came before it. Wing Josh Reed is among a group of players filing a lawsuit looking to get that fifth year to play. The status of that future is in limbo.

“I can’t talk about that stuff. I will say how everybody knows how much I love Josh Reed… he’s an impressive young man. He’s a great example of what we want our guys to be,” Rhoades said. “The rules change every day. If the judges (are) involved, they change by the minute. It just is what it is.”

Reed’s particular case is still in its early stages, but it’s a continuation of what we’ve seen. Former Penn State wing Puff Johnson was granted an injunction midseason last year to join the Ohio State Buckeyes for a brief stay.

Rhoades said this different college sports world made it difficult to develop players until they were upperclassmen, something that specifically pertains to the Nittany Lions, whose key freshmen are almost all departed.

When asked about the resources at his disposal, a frequent topic throughout last season and his entire tenure, Rhoades said Penn State is at “the bottom.”

“No coach is ever gonna say they have enough. Everybody wants more in this arms race. It is what it is, you got whatever you’re given,” Rhoades said. “The situation we’re in is what we’re in, and we gotta find a way to make the best of it and go from there.”
