title: Hobbies, chores to round out the summer
author: Samantha Cormier | For The Collegian
description:
There’s a certain anticipation of the fall semester at Penn State. Football games, new classes, extracurriculars, social activities and much more to look forward to. However, as summer break is almost over, students can take this opportunity to make the most of the calm before the storm.

As July finishes up and August is soon upon Penn Staters, here are some can’t-miss activities to round out the summer.

Start a new hobby

Starting a new skill is a great way to explore interests and to enter the year with new insights and more creativity.

Take a class in painting, photography, crocheting or hone a previous skill further. Exploring something new is another great way to create a community at Penn State, as numerous clubs exist for different hobbies.

Finish out that summer job strong

Whether it’s an internship, a retail job, a restaurant job or a babysitting gig, it’s important for students to finish out their summer jobs in an impactful way.

Send a thank you note to a boss, connect with co-workers on LinkedIn and keep all contact information for future job opportunities.

Get those finances in order

After working hard for a summer income, be sure to set aside some of the money from each paycheck to savings or a special fund dedicated to college.

Going back to school means spending money on new apartment decorations, breakfasts with new roommates and nights out with friends.

Setting some money aside, creating a savings account and cutting back on the mindless online shopping we’re all guilty of is a great way to get ahead.

Fix up that resumé

Summer is the perfect time to focus on updating a resumé.

Add new work experience along with any leadership roles or extracurricular involvement at Penn State. A bonus recommendation is to print multiple copies of the resumé to have on hand for career fairs and recruitment events at the beginning of the year.

Learn a professional skill

Take time to complete a certification or short course that can add a skill to a resumé.

Websites like LinkedIn Learning and Coursera have short courses that students can access and complete within just a few days. These websites have free and paid courses, so students can even learn a skill for no charge.

Catch up on summer reading

What used to be a forced task could be a great way to get ahead for the school year. Students can read a book that is in their field of study, or take time to leisurely read a book before the semester speeds up.

If you’re trying to ignore the fact that a plethora of assignments will fill your plate in the fall, escape with a fantasy novel. You could always pick up a romance and raise your expectations to unrealistic heights, too.

Get in the kitchen

Without parents cooking for students at school, summer is the perfect time to learn from family members or a Youtube video how to cook basic meals.

Coming into the school year with the knowledge of how to use the kitchen in an apartment, communal dorm or house is important to avoid spending money on takeout.

Volunteer for a good cause

Volunteering can fill up some empty spaces in your summer schedule while also giving back to your community.

Look up food pantries in your area and see if they’re accepting donations, and call some shelters to see what they need. Donating old clothes or household items is another simple way to give back.

Spend time in nature

Take some time away from digital devices and get out into nature. Hikes, runs, long walks or spending some time at a local park can help students de-stress before a busy year.

If you develop enough love for your new being-in-nature hobby before you come back to campus, Rothrock State Forest, Penn State’s Arboretum and the many hiking trails within Centre County’s mountains await you.

Take a vacation

Finally, take that last vacation to have a clear mind before the new year starts. Whether it’s a long weekend, a whole week or just a few hours, exploring a new city or country is the ultimate summer to-do.

title: Column | Study abroad blues
author: Lailah Acuña I The Daily Collegian
description:
However dramatic this sounds, upon returning from my six-week study abroad program in Mexico, I found myself feeling lost, sad and dull. Like something was missing from my life, like something had been stripped from me.

Before I left, I prepared myself mentally for the changes in environment, culture, language and routine I was about to face. I found navigating all of these things easy, though, because they’re the kinds of challenges the kind of thing people more commonly talk about.

I hadn’t been aware that my latest affliction would afflict me at all. I’ve since learned it’s dubbed the “study abroad blues:” When a person is overcome with sadness and emotional lows upon returning home from an extended time of studying abroad.

During my time in Mexico, I had essentially built a new identity. I had a new home with my host family, I was making friends in Mexico and I was building a life at the university I was attending. I began to feel more connected to my Latina heritage. Even though I’m not Mexican, I saw ways in which our cultures were shared.

Speaking Spanish lent largely to this, helping me heal some of my internal struggles with my cultural identity. And people were finally pronouncing my name right! While that may seem small, it made me feel incredibly validated. The people who get it get it. I felt like I belonged.

I loved the inexpensive food, artisan markets, walkable streets, town center, sense of community and warm hospitality. Just as quickly as these things fell into place, I fell out of that place; I had to return home. Forced into my old routine, being back in the United States meant I was without every single one of my favorite parts of Mexico.

I no longer felt that strong sense of acceptance or belonging. I didn’t feel motivated to go outside or explore — not that anything was within walking distance, anyway. No hanging out with the friends I had made in Mexico or with my host family. No bustling market streets and large, populated town centers. Tacos cost $15 instead of $5.

To say something dramatic once more, I was heartbroken. I couldn’t stop thinking about my old identity. I wanted to go back to Mexico just so I could finish building it.

But in that true, ever-optimistic American fashion so ingrained in this country’s culture, I found a light at the end of the tunnel. I remembered a conversation I had with my host mom, where I told her something along the lines of, “Life here is so energetic and vibrant, everything has character. In the U.S., everything is boring. I don’t want to go back.”

I remember her smirking and shaking her head to the side. She told me her life — the market streets, people taking up as much space as possible in town centers, cheap tacos — was actually quite boring and repetitive. Had it been her visiting the States, she probably would’ve gotten that same rush of dopamine I did in Mexico.

My perspective was very one-sided. Things I saw as better only felt better because it was my first time experiencing them. Every day I thought to myself, “If I lived here, I would never get bored,” there were plenty of people living there, getting bored.

Suddenly going back to my home, something I experienced my entire life, meant I derived little excitement from it. Experiencing something for my entire life meant I was bound to have a crash, and returning to stagnancy after having experienced something new and stimulating is what kick-started the blues.

These feelings made me dwell on the past, but I like to think of them now as proof I’ve gained new appreciation for things others may overlook. Everyone’s post-study abroad emotions differ, and the blues might never be part of your emotional color palette at all. Whatever thoughts you find circling your mind after your study abroad, it’s important to realize that change is good, even though it’s difficult, because it gives you a perspective on life that is uniquely yours.

What I realized is that I never lost a part of myself, even though it really felt like it. Instead, new parts of myself have filled in where I thought that was. They’re full of love for the dull things, and they’re anything but the color blue.

title: Closet staples for fall sweater weather
author: Anisa Daniel-Oniko | The Daily Collegian
description:
The fall semester is quickly approaching, and with it colder weather. While Penn Staters may miss the warmer weather and its wardrobe options, fall in State College doesn’t require you to sacrifice style.

Here are some things to hang up in your closet this fall.

Long-sleeved tops

If you don’t have any long-sleeved tops in your rotation, now’s the time to go shopping. A good long-sleeved top can be worn with jeans, trousers or skirts and can be layered over lighter clothing options.

A basic button down is great, but you have other options. For more of an exciting twist, seek out asymmetrical shirts, butterfly sleeves or shirts with metal eyelets. Pay attention to the fabrics you choose, as this will determine how much layering you will need to do.

Jackets

The key to fall is layers. A jacket is the perfect way to add warmth to an outfit without sacrificing structure or style. Try denim for a durable option that goes with anything, or leather for a stylistic edge.

Turtlenecks

These balance fashion and functionality and are easily layered. Try layering a button down shirt over a turtleneck, or replicate the Steve Jobs classic by pairing a black turtleneck with blue jeans.

Don’t be afraid to play around with fabrics, but keep an eye out for knit, which balances breathability with warmth.

Scarves

Irrespective of print, pattern or style, scarves are a fall fashion staple for a reason.

Scarves come in a range of fabric options, lengths and colorways, but lighter options may be preferable for the months preceding winter.

A chunky scarf can add dimension and warmth to your layers, while experimenting with colors or fabrics can change the visual or textural profile of your outfit.

Boots

Suede, leather, square-toed, pointed, black or brown, there are so many styles of boots, which are an incredibly chic way to elevate an outfit and keep your feet warm.

In order to find a statement boot, try experimenting with profile and height — slouchy, thigh-high boots with a skinny heel or stiff, ankle-length boots with a chunky wedge — or distinctive details like buckles or zippers.

Tank tops or baby tees

Don’t be so quick to stash away everything from your summer wardrobe.

Tank tops and baby tees may seem thin, but they can be layered easily. A basic tank top or baby tee can go under a jacket, adding dynamic twists to your usual wardrobe rotations. A tank top can also add a pop of color under a light, gauzy shirt.

If you’ve had a good summer with your tank tops and tees, rinse, restyle and repeat.

Tights

Tights are another good way to give your summer favorites a lift. If you want to wear something on the shorter side — miniskirts, minidresses or shorts — going for tights provides an extra layer for warmth without compromising your overall look.

Sheer tights are available if you like an invisible finish, while colored tights can add a maximalist flair to your outfits.

Statement hoodies

Hoodies are a fall semester must, but they don’t have to be boring. Seek out a hoodie that speaks to you in some way, with a slogan, pattern, fun fabric or design. You can take inspiration from streetwear, band tees, sports and anything else that’s graphically interesting.

If you’re feeling especially full of Penn State pride, consider getting a Nittany Lion inspired hoodie from The Family Clothesline, Lions Pride or Nittany Outlet.

Jewelry

Figure out if you like gold tones, silver tones or both and find jewelry to match. Accessories can be a fun way to break up the monotony of an outfit, especially when you’re working with layers or baggy silhouettes.

Try to find interesting pieces to make your outfit stand out. A solid bracelet, ring stack or an oversized pair of earrings can give an overall lift to your look.

title: Off the record | Scared Susie
author: Miss Behave I The Daily Collegian
description:
Editor’s Note: Off the record is a weekly column written by a fourth-year Collegian staffer under an alias. It aims to promote a space for honest conversations about love, sex and relationships. Those interested in sharing their experiences or submitting a topic can do so through this anonymous form.

Dear Susie,

Freshman year is filled with so much freedom and change you're not going to know what to do with yourself, but that doesn’t mean you're not right to worry.

I’ll admit, it’s a lot at once: you no longer live with your parents, your friends aren’t a car ride away and you might be learning to live with a stranger. The good thing, though, is that the uncomfortableness fades.

I’m going to be blunt, but you need to hear it. You’re going to become a different person. You’re going to go home for the first time and feel out of place in your childhood bedroom. The living room couch you used to lounge across won’t feel as comfy to spend a lazy afternoon on. Your kitchen will seem foreign.

You can have your reservations, but don’t become burdened by the unknowns. If you leave college the same person you were going into it, you didn’t do it right.

Changing and losing yourself aren’t interchangeable. You can become a version of yourself that feels unrecognizable yet still relies on the same morals you consider essential to your being.

If the people in your life can't accept the new you, the version of you that’s growing and evolving, that’s on them. It’s not fair to stunt your social and personal development to please people. You should surround yourself with people who are OK with all versions of you, and college is the perfect place to do that; there're countless people sitting right next to you in class who are carrying the exact same weight and anxiety.

Maybe your hometown friends don’t like that you have a new group of friends or enjoy things you didn’t previously, but oh well. It’s not reasonable to expect you not to have new interests or people in your life when you're in a space that encourages and warrants just that.

Don’t close yourself off because you fear the possible repercussions of how people are going to perceive you when you go home. There have been plenty of times when I’ve thought, “I would have never done this in high school,” or “that one friend would hate this.” You can’t act on the what-ifs.

If you think you’re not going to lose friends, you’re likely wrong. Whether it be growing apart from a lack of communication, or realizing they're not the type of person you want around anymore, some of your friends may become a distant memory. It’s a canon event. If it happens, don’t feel ashamed, or like there’s something wrong with you. The friends you want to keep will stick around.

I want so badly to tell you that the first people you meet at college are going to be your bridesmaids, but I would be lying. It might be your roommate or your next-door neighbor; you inevitably think you’ve found your people. The people in your proximity aren’t your only options; with time comes fresh faces and opportunities for authentic relationships. Once you find a group of friends that aren’t bonded by being lonely freshmen, the true fun begins.

My first week, I met this girl who lived on my floor, and we did everything together for the first couple of weeks. Dinner, walks on campus. We even joined the same club.

Fast forward three years, and we see each other, smile, and continue walking. It really doesn’t have to be awkward; our friendship served its purpose for the time being, and we began spending time with people who were better suited for us.

Although you may feel a little fake going through friends, it doesn’t make you a bad person. You have to spend time with a lot of different types of people to find the people you actually want to spend your precious free time with.

You’re going to change an insurmountable amount in college, and you have to lean into it. I get that you’re scared and worried you'll become a version of yourself that doesn't feel normal, but it’ll be OK. If you lead with your core values and remain true to what makes you you, everything else will work itself out.

College is your time to take risks, try new things, meet new people and grow into the person you’re meant to become, the person you dreamed about when you were 7-years-old with your eyes glued to some cool, college-aged character on TV.

Be kind to yourself as you enter your freshman year, and trust your gut. The rest will follow suit.

Until next time,

Miss Behave

title: For former Penn State athletes, Randy Jepson’s legacy is family, success
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
After 45 years at Penn State, men’s gymnastics Randy Jepson has passed the reins to Tony Beck.

Three National Coach of the Year honors and three national championships comprise Jepson’s career, but behind those accolades is Jepson’s coaching of Olympians and walk-on athletes alike. He spent 35 years as head coach building up his team’s gymnastics abilities, but he built up a family in them, too.

That sense of family was so strong that a photo of Josh Borromeo’s parents wearing Penn State wigs and face paint during the 2007 NCAA Championship, where Borromeo competed for the Nittany Lions, still sits on Jepson’s mantle two decades later.

“He really brought us together as a group, as a team and as a family,” Josh said. “For me, for my other teammates, when my brother was on the team and for the parents and everyone involved in the program, that’s something we’re going to cherish for our lifetime.”

Before each school year, Jepson and his wife, Sue Jepson, welcomed the team into their home, and as the years went on, those meals and memories became the foundation of his program, Josh said.

Jepson coached his team to 14 individual national champions and developed eight Olympians, the most recent being Stephen Nedoroscik. He helped his student-athletes grow both as gymnasts and leaders beyond the sport.

Josh’s younger brother, Brayden Borromeo, who was also coached by Jepson at Penn State, said Jepson is a legend for the length and success of his career.

“If you want to talk about legacy, look at all the guys that had come through the program during his tenure, and look at where they are now,” Brayden said. “He has guys leading industries all over the world, in both gymnastics as well as every aspect of life. It's a testament to what Randy taught as a person to become a leader, in whatever respective career that you chose.”

Jepson’s influence, many said, shaped the husbands, fathers, leaders and professionals they became after their competitive careers. Brayden said his wife often reminds him of Jepson’s impact on the team, and added that Jepson is a “molder of men.”

Despite coming in as a lower-rated recruit, Jepson recognized Tristan Duverglas’ potential. Duverglas played an instrumental role in Penn State’s 2015 Big Ten Championship team after growing to become team captain and first team All-America his senior year.

“Randy did everything in his power to see the best in us and show us that anything was possible,” Duverglas said. “You can bring a group of people together from all these different walks of life — in different countries, different cities — and have them fall in love with the school and a program and just continue to fall in love with the sport.”

Throughout the years, Jepson’s program experienced its fair share of highs and lows. Along with four Big Ten titles and three national championships came years in which the program struggled to compete at the top of the conference.

Noah Roberson, who competed for Penn State from 2015 to 2018, said it was great having Jepson in his corner, and credits his success both in the gym and classroom to his former coach.

When the team didn’t live up to expectations of success, Roberson said, Jepson took it personally.

“It wasn’t all sunshine and rainbows,” Roberson said. “He would always communicate the standard of excellence that was expected, and we were all striving to reach that.”

After a seven-year drought, the Nittany Lions won the 2015 Big Ten Championship at Rec Hall, a moment that ranks among the favorites among former athletes. Duverglas said being able to hold the trophy up with Jepson was a top moment for him.

“His passion for the sport transferred to a lot of us as we continued to train and go through our years at Penn State,” Duverglas said.

While at Penn State, Jepson was also the faculty advisor for Penn State Christian Athletics (PCSA), an organization created in 2010 for Christian student-athletes.

Maddie Ullom and Collin Burkhart, both former Penn State track and field athletes, worked with Jepson in PSCA as officers.

“He was more than a coach. He’s somebody I could trust and somebody I could come to for advice,” Burkhart said.

Jepson “lived a very pure and Christian life” those in PCSA tried to emulate, according to Burkhart. Whether someone was a national champion or walk-on, Burkhart said Jepson treated everyone the same.

Ullom said he and Sue set an example of a Godly relationship and taught them the essence of “living biblically.”

“He always tells us how he was as an athlete and how hardcore he was, and that comes across in his coaching style and when he talks to us about athletics,” Ullom said. “The difference, at the end of the day, is that he still loves us. Not because of our athletic ability, but just because of who we are as followers of Christ.”

title: 4 sleepers in Penn State’s 2027 recruiting class
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Tyler Warren was a 3-star recruit before becoming a John Mackey Award winner, a first-round NFL draft pick and one of Penn State’s all-time greatest tight ends. Trace McSorley was also below the 4-star threshold, and went on to win the 2016 Big Ten championship as a sophomore, Penn State’s first in eight years.

Needless to say, the stars don’t tell the full story. College football has seen 5-star prospects crumble under the pressure, and programs develop diamonds in the rough who weren’t notable out of high school.

Out of Penn State’s 15 total 3-star commits, here are four sleepers who could exceed expectations in Penn State’s 2027 recruiting class.

TE Sean Currie

Sean Currie has everything he needs to be a premier tight end. He’s 6-foot-7, and 230 pounds, but he doesn’t let his size slow him down, remaining a mobile, agile receiving option that uses his length as an advantage.

Currie’s long arms make him a viable option as both a receiver and as a blocker. He has shown through his film that he’s able to create separation to make catches and leverage his wingspan to force opponents far off their mark.

Currently, the 3-star recruit is ranked as the No. 16 player out of New Jersey and No. 30 tight end in the Class of 2027, per 247Sports composite.

Despite not earning the fourth star, Currie’s a developing tight end that has the framework required of him to learn collegiate-level football.

Currie is one of two committed tight ends in the 2027 class alongside 4-star recruit Cooper Terwilliger. It’ll be an interesting position battle for a higher spot on the depth chart between the pair when they arrive on campus, as the star rating doesn’t always paint the clearest picture.

QB Will Wood

With 4-star Massachusetts quarterback Peter Bourque and Penn State target committing to Virginia Tech, Campbell didn’t look too far to find his signal caller for the 2027 class in Will Wood.

Wood, a 3-star from Westwood, Massachusetts, flew under the radar, with his top college choices being Penn State, Boston College and Arkansas.

The No. 3 player out of his home state, Wood spearheaded Xaverian Brothers High School to back-to-back MIAA Division I Super Bowl victories as the starter. He’s poised in the high-pressure moments, evidenced by his ability to win close battles against Xaverian’s archnemesis, St. John’s Prep, through calm decision-making and execution of crucial plays.

Wood is the kind of quarterback that fits Campbell’s scheme. Like Rocco Becht, Wood is proficient in staying patient in the pocket, but expertly rolls to the outside when he needs space. Both are known for their consistent good decisions, leadership roles and being the quiet driving force behind their respective offenses.

Campbell developed Becht from a 3-star recruit and the No. 33 quarterback in the 2022 class, into a Power Four starter. With Wood displaying a near-identical prospect ranking, Campbell and Jake Waters have the potential to craft a star passer with a pension for winning no matter the odds.

IOL Jon Sassic

Campbell made a step in the right direction toward securing a foothold in Pennsylvania recruiting with 3-star offensive lineman Jon Sassic.

Coming in at 6-foot-6 and 285 pounds, Ryan Clanton will likely want Sassic to bulk up in order to play at the collegiate level, and he possesses the frame to make that a reality. The No. 38 player in Pennsylvania could use the extra weight to become one of Penn State’s starting offensive guards in just a few years, judging by how physical Sassic is on the line right now.

Part of what makes Sassic an appealing recruit is his tenacity and how he buries opponents into the ground. He stands to gain a lot of raw power by using Penn State’s facilities after one more year of high school to refine his skills on the line.

LS Clayton Powell

The long snapper is one of the most crucial pieces of any kicking lineup, and no one snaps the ball better in the 2027 class than Clayton Powell.

Although he wasn’t ranked on 247Sports composite prior to his commitment to Penn State, Powell is now the No. 59 player out of Louisiana and the No. 1 long snapper in the Class of 2027. He only had two other offers on the board — Arkansas and McNeese — before Penn State offered him in June.

As long snapping is a position without too much depth, noting that Penn State currently has two rostered long snappers in redshirt sophomore Andrew Dufault and redshirt senior Blaise Sokach-Minnick, Powell may be on the fast track to running the position for an extended period of time.

Powell, like with many other position groups at Penn State, will be entering a professional-grade legacy. Tyler Duzansky and Chris Stoll are two recent examples of Nittany Lion long snappers to go to the NFL after standout Nittany Lion careers.

title: How to follow soccer after 2026 World Cup
author: Myles Hannak | The Daily Collegian
description:
The 2026 FIFA World Cup, which garnered unprecedented spectacle both on and off the pitch, is officially over. World No. 2 and tournament favorite Spain defeated top-ranked Argentina.

With the whole world watching, a grueling, deadlocked game carried into extra time until Ferran Torres netted the decisive goal. Argentina was led by the legendary Lionel Messi, who carried the team to victory in the 2022 World Cup, a game that already holds its own space in history.

Now that the pageantry on United States soil has concluded for the first time since 1994, some red, white and blue supporters are wondering what’s next for a game that seemingly experienced more attention than ever in the States.

For all the Yankees out there who are new to soccer, fútbol, or whatever you’d like to call it, here’s how you can keep up with the sport until the World Cup to tick back around in 2030.

Clubs, leagues to watch

When international play isn’t around, players typically appear with a club side in the form of a domestic league, domestic cup and international cup against the top teams in their region, not just their country. The U.S. has its own league, which kicked off on July 16, just three days before the World Cup final.

Major League Soccer (MLS) features big names, like Messi, Robert Lewandowski, Antoine Griezmann and Thomas Müller, but it also nurtures some of the stars and stripes

future prospects for the national team. Touted 16-year-old Cavan Sullivan, who plays for the Philadelphia Union, has a rumored move to English club giant Manchester City in the works.

Besides MLS, there’s also the United Soccer League and USL2, which operates in a promotion/relegation system, a format that resembles the top leagues across the world, yet has not been adapted to include the MLS; it operates independently, besides matchups in the U.S. Open Cup, when the two organizations meet.

The English Premier League currently stands as the pinnacle for club competition. Teams like Manchester City, Manchester United, Arsenal, Chelsea, Tottenham and Liverpool historically represent the biggest the country has to offer. It’s extremely competitive at the top, as placements for international competition are seeded based on a squad’s final table finish. Last season, Arsenal claimed the pole position for their first League Title in over two decades.

Although those six represent the titans, two other English clubs, Aston Villa and Crystal Palace, stand as the only international champions from the country in the UEFA Europa League and Conference League, their respective competitions.

The UEFA Champions League joins that pair as the tournament to determine the best European club squad. It was claimed in consecutive years by French juggernaut Paris Saint-Germain, who has held a monopoly on the domestic league, winning it five times straight.

Most other domestic leagues resemble that of the French League One, with a stark drop-off from the top. The German Bundesliga is routinely dominated by FC Bayern Munich, while FC Barcelona holds back-to-back Spanish league titles, only flipping in recent years with Real Madrid and in the Italian League Juventus holds 16 more titles than anyone else, but hasn’t done so since 2019–20.

Women’s World Cup

If you have a knack for international ball and club competition just isn’t your thing, you’re just in luck, as the Women’s World Cup resumes in the summer of 2027, from June 24 to July 25.

The competition will take place in Brazil and last tournament’s winner, Spain, is entering as the early favorite. Despite past successes, the United States women’s national soccer team doesn’t enter as a top-14 squad in this competition, according to ESPN.

NCAA Soccer

College sports always bring a great twist on professional sports, and that’s no different in soccer. The NCAA level is experiencing not only a whirlwind of change, but exponential development as well.

The DI cabinet officially ruled that the men’s season will be two semesters long next year, a change wanted among the college soccer fandom. There will now be a College Cup played to match this new format, which is closer to the professional leagues.

For Penn State specifically, this couldn’t come at a better time. New coach Rob Dow has already stayed busy on the recruiting trail to build a roster for the men’s team; and the long-term home of the Nittany Lions women's and men’s soccer teams, Jeffrey Field, underwent an offseason of renovations.

Anyone in Happy Valley over the winter months saw the massive white bubble of an athletic complex the university was renting. This structure allowed players to train during the harsh cold months, and the time to see if it's been helpful is just around the corner.

title: Socios announces partnership with Penn State Athletics
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State will be part of a groundbreaking advancement in fan engagement.

Socios.com, a sports tokenization platform, announced the first five teams included in its college programme in partnership with Playfly Sports. Those teams are Penn State, LSU, Maryland, Michigan State and Texas A&M.

There are plans for the company to expand its partnership up to 30 college teams over the next 12 months.

Through what Socios.com dubs "Fan Tokens," fans are able to stake currency on their favorite teams to earn Reward Points for "new engagement experiences, rewards and access," according to the company's website. Portions of the generated revenue is used to support schools' Name, Image and Likeness (NIL) funds.

Rewards for stakeholders include VIP tickets and "exclusive team experiences" that fans can use their Reward Points to bid for.

"The company’s vision is to create a global fan network where supporters are active members of digital communities and can engage more deeply with the teams they love," Socios.com stated in the official release.

Socios.com already partners with over 70 teams in sports such as soccer, eSports, fighting, motorsports and rugby.

title: Former Penn State wide receiver Julian Fleming sentenced after fatal ATV accident
author: Elliott Inscho | Sports Editor
description:
Former Penn State football wide receiver Julian Crushshon-Fleming was sentenced to nine to 23 months in Bradford County Correctional Facility on Monday, according to a press release from Bradford County District Attorney Richard Wilson.

Crushshon-Fleming, 25, of Elysburg, Pennslylvania, pleaded guilty to charges of involuntary manslaughter and driving under the influence in April after an ATV accident on May 23, 2025 that killed his girlfriend, Alyssa Boyd, a passenger in the vehicle.

Fleming was driving an ATV with a blood alcohol concentration of .118, exceeding the legal limit of .08, according to court documents. The press release said the ATV hit a deer.

“While we were confident that we could prove Crushshon-Fleming committed a DUI offense, proving the connection between that and the death of the victim would be difficult,” Wilson said in the release. “While Crushshon-Fleming’s intoxication did not help matters, a jury would likely conclude that the collision with the deer caused the riders to crash, and therefore the victim’s death, not the alcohol intoxication … Manslaughter is therefore an appropriate resolution.”

Crushshon-Fleming, a former five-star recruit, began his college football career with Ohio State in 2020. He played four seasons with the Buckeyes before transferring to Penn State in 2024.
